output_json.patch_notes:
Root-cause fix in src/main/java/net/sf/mpxj/common/InputStreamHelper.java: added a private static validateZipEntryDestination(File dir, File file) helper that canonicalizes both `dir` and the entry's resolved `file`, and throws IOException if `file`'s canonical path is not equal to, or a strict descendant of, `dir`'s canonical path (using File.separator-based prefix check, which also blocks absolute-path entry names since those still canonicalize outside `dir`). This call was inserted right after `File file = new File(dir, entry.getName())` (originally line 126), before the code branches into the directory-entry mkdirsQuietly(file) path, the parent mkdirsQuietly(parent) path, and the FileOutputStream(file) write path — covering all three sink traces in the alert with one check.

Added a new regression test file src/test/java/net/sf/mpxj/common/InputStreamHelperTest.java covering: (1) a simple "../evil.txt" file-entry traversal, (2) a nested-path traversal where an earlier zip entry creates a real "sub/" directory and a later entry "sub/../../evil.txt" walks back out through it (chosen because a bare single-entry nested-".." pattern incidentally throws FileNotFoundException even on unpatched code, due to how File.mkdirs()/FileOutputStream resolve non-existent intermediate path segments — this two-entry ordering reproduces genuine escape as flagged in the alert's regression_hint about ordering-dependent sequences within one archive), (3) a "../evil-dir/" directory-entry traversal exercising the mkdirsQuietly(file) sink that never reaches FileOutputStream, and (4) a normal non-traversal entry to confirm legitimate extraction still works. Each traversal test independently computes the canonical target the vulnerable code would have written and asserts it does not exist after extraction (or that extraction throws), so the tests are entry-name-driven rather than relying on a hardcoded escape location.

Verified via git stash: with InputStreamHelper.java reverted to the original vulnerable version, all 3 traversal tests fail (3 failures) confirming they genuinely exercise the vulnerability; with the fix restored, all 4 tests pass, and `mvn -B -DskipTests package` builds cleanly.
output_json.risk_notes: The fix throws IOException for any zip entry whose resolved path canonicalizes outside the target extraction directory, which changes behavior only for malicious/malformed archives — legitimate archives (entries with relative, non-escaping paths) are unaffected, as shown by the passing testNonTraversalEntryIsExtracted case. writeZipStreamToTempDir() only catches ZipException specifically, so this new IOException propagates to callers exactly as other I/O failures during extraction already did (e.g. a permission-denied mkdir), meaning no new exception-handling contract is introduced. Canonicalization (getCanonicalPath) also incidentally guards against symlink-based escapes noted in the alert's bypass list, since it resolves real paths rather than doing purely lexical normalization. One residual consideration: the check runs per-entry using the entry's own resolved path at processing time, so if a prior entry in the same archive created a symlink that a later entry's path traverses through, canonicalization at the time of the later check still resolves through that real (now-existing) symlink and enforces containment against it — the ordering-dependent regression test added here exercises the closely-related "real intermediate directory from an earlier entry" scenario.
output_json.summary: Fixed a Zip Slip / path traversal vulnerability (CWE-22) in InputStreamHelper.processZipStream(). The method built extraction destinations directly from untrusted ZipEntry names (`new File(dir, entry.getName())`) with no containment check, letting a malicious archive entry (e.g. "../evil.txt", nested "sub/../../evil.txt", or a "../"-laden directory entry) write files or create directories outside the sandboxed temp extraction directory. Added a single root-cause guard, `validateZipEntryDestination(dir, file)`, called immediately after the `File file = new File(dir, entry.getName())` construction at line 126/127 — before either code path (directory-entry mkdirsQuietly, parent mkdirsQuietly, or FileOutputStream) executes. The guard canonicalizes both the extraction directory and the resolved entry path and throws an IOException unless the entry's canonical path equals or is a strict descendant of the directory's canonical path. Because all three sinks named in the alert (mkdirsQuietly(file) for directory entries, mkdirsQuietly(parent) for file entries, and new FileOutputStream(file)) derive from the same `file` value computed at that one line, this single check blocks all of them, including bypass variants such as mid-path "../" traversal, absolute-path entries, and directory-entry-only traversal.
